plates.quality_reason: Quality: readable faces (Norwegian-American physiologist Per Fredrik Scholander and Harold T. Hammel in the California redwood forest on 16 April 1965 aiming a .22 hunting rifle at the 82-metre crown of a coast redwood Sequoia sempervirens and testing the shot twig in their steel pressure bomb reading -15 to -17 atmospheres).

In a sun-dappled 1965 California redwood grove, Per Scholander and Harold Hammel collect a freshly shot high redwood twig and seal it into a cylindrical steel pressure chamber with its cut stem protruding as the brass gauge reads fifteen atmospheres. teach_overlay.scale: Per Scholander's pressure bomb works like measuring how hard a stretched elastic band was pulling by seeing how many kilograms of weight it takes to push the snapped end back to the starting line — proving desert bushes pull water with eighty atmospheres of suction, enough negative pressure to suck fresh water straight out of salty ocean mud
